author: harness:claude-code

patch.value: As a coding agent, every pm command I run costs the fewest tokens that still fully answer my question, and I can see what I spent

The token-efficiency work is spread across a budget contract, an encoding study, intent-scoped projections, a diagnostics budget, per-invocation accounting, delta reads, and a transcript-replay gate. Each is individually correct and none of them states the entitlement they collectively serve, so nothing checks the composite: an agent could gain a cheaper encoding while losing a needed field, or gain intent projections while diagnostics stay unbounded, and every individual gate would still pass. State it from the consumer's side. An agent asking a question should receive an answer whose token cost is proportional to the information it actually needs, never to the size of the workspace or the verbosity of the command; should never pay for fields it discards; should pay a bounded, predictable amount when a command fails; and should be able to see, at any moment, what its context budget was spent on. The composite is measurable end to end as tokens per completed task, which is the only number that captures all of it at once.

Tokens per completed task is measured over a representative agent-task corpus and tracked release over release as the composite figure; A component change that improves its own metric while raising the composite fails, proven by a deliberate negative-control scenario; The corpus covers the small-workspace, large-workspace, failing-command, and returning-agent cases, so no scenario is optimized at another's expense; An agent can obtain a per-invocation breakdown of what its budget was spent on without leaving its normal loop; No command's answer omits a field the corpus tasks actually consume, asserted by a completeness check rather than by reviewer judgment; The composite figure is published with the release so the trend is externally visible rather than internal-only
State and measure the agent-side entitlement that the whole token-efficiency programme exists to deliver
Composite entitlements fail at the seams; tokens per completed task is the only measure an agent's operator actually experiences
Adds an end-to-end measure over existing gates and makes a regression in the composite visible even when every component gate passes
Token efficiency has one acceptance surface measured as tokens per completed task, not seven independently green gates

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
First composite baseline for this entitlement, measured 2026-07-27 on the shipped 2026.7.26 build against this repository's own 2,113-item tracker. The acceptance criteria ask for tokens per completed task tracked release over release and no baseline had been recorded, so this is the number to move.

Output bytes, human-readable default format, one invocation each. Token estimates are bytes divided by four.

  contracts --summary                4,193 B    ~1.0k tok
  context --limit 10                 6,330 B    ~1.6k tok
  next --limit 5                     8,887 B    ~2.2k tok
  get <item> (default depth)         4,532 B    ~1.1k tok
  get <item> --depth brief           4,491 B    ~1.1k tok
  list-open --limit 20               4,517 B    ~1.1k tok
  search <phrase> --limit 5          1,970 B    ~0.5k tok
  deps <item> --format context       6,486 B    ~1.6k tok
  graph impact <item> --summary        229 B    ~0.06k tok
  stats                                439 B    ~0.1k tok
  validate                          22,407 B    ~5.6k tok
  root help                         13,542 B    ~3.4k tok
  create --help                      7,818 B    ~2.0k tok
  update --help                      8,261 B    ~2.1k tok

Composite for the canonical orientation loop an agent runs before it has done any work — contracts summary, context, next, then reading the one item it picked — is 23,942 B, roughly 6.0k tokens. That is the floor, and it assumes the agent already knows the command names. An agent that reads root help first pays 13,542 B more, and one that reads the help for the two commands it will mutate with pays another 16,079 B, which takes a cold start to roughly 13.4k tokens before a single useful mutation.

Three observations the individual component items do not state.

One. Diagnostics dominate. A single pm validate costs more than the entire orientation loop, and it is the command an agent is most likely to run when something is already wrong, which is exactly when its remaining budget is smallest. This is the composite evidence for pm-cha95z and it is stronger than the per-command case: the diagnostic is not merely large, it is larger than everything the agent did to get to the point of needing it.

Two. Help is a third of the cold start and is governed by nothing. The command and flag surfaces have owners and budgets, and the help rendered from them does not.

Three. The depth ladder does not help a leaf. On a Story with six dependencies and no children, brief and default differ by 41 bytes, under one percent. The ladder is sized by children, so the reduction an agent expects from asking for less does not arrive on the items it most often reads. That is not a defect in the ladder, it is evidence that depth is the wrong axis for the common case and that the intent-scoped projections on pm-cxr0jb are the mechanism that would actually pay here.

Re-measure this block each time a component lands and record the delta, since the point of this entitlement is that a component win that raises the composite is a loss.

value.author: harness:opencode
value.text:
Warm steady-state loop baseline (measured 2026-07-27 on 2026.7.27 against the 2,128-item tracker, extends the 2026-07-26 cold-start baseline). Cold start is paid once per session; the warm loop — orient, read, mutate, confirm — is paid hundreds of times per agent-session and dominates lifetime token cost, so this is the number the entitlement is actually scored on.

Measured warm primitives: mutation comment envelope 1,447 B (~360 tok); get --depth brief on a leaf Task 2,890 B (~720 tok); get --fields id,status 48 B (~12 tok); update --id-only 38 B (~10 tok); context --limit 5 4,051 B (~1.0k tok).

Two facts fall out. First, the cheap path already exists end to end: a disciplined agent can run its entire warm loop — projected reads and id-only mutation envelopes — for tens of bytes per cycle, roughly two orders of magnitude under the default-envelope loop (~4.3k B for read+mutate). Nothing new needs to be invented for the floor; the flags ship today. Second, the default path and the cheap path differ by ~100x and nothing steers an agent from one to the other: the entitlement failure is not capability, it is routing. An agent that never learned --fields/--id-only pays default prices forever.

That reframes the work this story binds. pm-cxr0jb (intent-scoped projections) is the routing fix done right: the declared intent picks the projection, so the cheap path stops depending on flag memorization. pm-5t33or (declared output budgets) is the ceiling that keeps defaults honest. pm-t5dt4z (self-reported accounting) is what makes the 100x spread visible at runtime instead of in a retrospective note. And the two-call cold start (pm-ka6d) is where the routing knowledge itself should be published, because a contract that says 'declare intent, receive floor' is one sentence an agent reads once and saves kilobytes per cycle for the rest of the session. Target state for the entitlement, stated as a number to move: warm loop under 200 B per orient-read-mutate-confirm cycle by default-routed intent, with the current 4.3k B default loop as the baseline to beat.
